newsitem.title: USA: Judge denies Hilton request for ITT annual meeting.
newsitem.headline: Judge denies Hilton request for ITT annual meeting.

text.p: A federal judge Monday denied a motion by Hilton Hotels Corp. to force ITT Corp. to hold its annual meeting in mid-May, ending Hilton's attempt to force a quick shareholder vote on its $6.5 billion hostile bid for ITT.
The two companies have been battling in U.S. District Court in Las Vegas, Nevada, since Hilton proposed the deal in late January, which ITT snubbed shortly thereafter.

Beverly Hills-based Hilton wanted the annual meeting to take place quickly so ITT's shareholders could vote on a Hilton-nominated slate of directors before ITT could sell assets and change the company's structure.

Hilton argued that the state law of Nevada, where New York-based ITT is incorporated, requires an annual meeting no later than 12 months from the previous year's. ITT held its 1996 meeting on May 14 and has regularly held it in mid-May for 20 years.

ITT, however, countered that Nevada state law does not require a meeting every 12 months, and it said its bylaws allow it to postpone the meeting for 18 months, or until mid-November. ITT has yet to set a meeting date.

In his ruling, U.S. District Judge Philip Pro sided with ITT, citing one affidavit filed in the case that says the term "annual meeting" is a commonly used adjective to distinguish between a regular shareholder meeting and a special meeting.

He also said Nevada statutes allow a company to delay its meeting where no meeting has yet been scheduled, and added Hilton has failed to demonstrate that ITT has not met its fiduciary responsibility to shareholders by failing to schedule a meeting.

"We are pleased Judge Pro has rejected Hilton's attempt to change Nevada law," said ITT spokesman Jim Gallagher. "ITT remains on a course to deliver superior value for shareholders by operating our core lodging and gaming properties while realizing the full value of our non-core assets," he said.
In a statement, Hilton Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach said the company is not backing away from its $55-per-share bid for ITT.

"ITT's delay of its annual meeting in no way changes the fact that Hilton has put a compelling offer on the table," he said. "We are committed to making this transaction a reality, and look forward to taking this matter directly to ITT's shareholders to decide for themselves how best to create value for their investment in ITT."
Hilton launched its two-step, cash-and-stock offer for ITT in late January. Including debt assumption, the offer totaled $10.5 billion.

ITT rejected the offer in early February, calling it inadequate. The New York-based company's stock had traded as high as $65 per share in June, 1996, but had eroded to about $42.50 when Hilton made its offer.
ITT shares closed Monday down 37.5 cents at $58.75, while Hilton's stock ended off 37.5 cents at $25.375, both in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
To defend against Hilton's takeover attempt, ITT has been selling some assets and saying it will focus on its Sheraton brand hotels and Caesars casinos.

ITT has sold its stake in French telecommunications company Alcatel Alsthom for about $830 million and agreed to sell its 50 percent stake in Madison Square Garden Inc., owner of the famous New York sports arena and the New York Knicks basketball and Rangers hockey teams, for $650 million.
Analysts speculated ITT would use the money to issue a large cash dividend to shareholders or, more likely, buy back a huge portion of its own stock to thwart Hilton's bid.
For its part, Hilton has launched a proxy contest for control of ITT's board of directors, asking ITT shareholders to vote for Hilton-nominated directors at their next meeting.
